new responsibility here is deciding what to retain when extracting or rejecting.
All numerical inputs describe synthetic receivers, not measured performance.

## Hypotheses, correlation and a decision {#sec-detection-correlation}

Fix the receiver configuration, reference epoch, observation operator and valid
acquisition state. Let $\mathbf x\in\mathbb C^M$ contain peak-scaled complex
voltage observations after that operator: samples, channel outputs or selected
linear coefficients. A known dimensionless template $\mathbf a$ contains its
waveform, geometric response and calibrated phase orientation. It applies only
over the stated band, geometry, loading and calibration history. Test

$$
 H_0:\ \mathbf x=\mathbf n,\qquad
 H_1:\ \mathbf x=A\mathbf a+\mathbf n,
$$

where $A>0$ is a specified peak-voltage amplitude for the simple alternative.
Assume centered, jointly proper complex Gaussian noise with known positive
definite covariance $\mathbf C=E[\mathbf n\mathbf n^H]$ in V², identical under
both hypotheses. “Proper” means the complementary covariance $E[\mathbf n\mathbf n^T]$
vanishes; Gaussianity then supplies circular quadrature statistics. Chapter 9
can construct $\mathbf C$, but neither a covariance nor a noise figure establishes
the Gaussian distribution. Impulsive interference, clipping, uncertain covariance
or signal-dependent noise requires another likelihood or a qualified detector.

The interfaces need an explicit normalization. Chapter 8's field-to-voltage map
has units metres when driven in V/m. Choose a specified nonzero reference
responsivity in metres: its magnitude converts incident field amplitude to the
voltage $A$, while the normalized dimensionless $\mathbf a$ retains relative
channel, phase and waveform response. That reference is a model input or an
external calibration result, not something electronic injection alone establishes.
For stationary peak-envelope output noise with voltage spectral matrix
$\mathbf S_z(\nu)$ from Chapter 9, define a row observation kernel
$\mathbf b_i(t)$ in s⁻¹ acting on the centered output noise $\mathbf z_n(t)$:

$$
 n_i=\int \mathbf b_i(t)\mathbf z_n(t)\,dt,\qquad
 \mathbf B_i(\nu)=\int \mathbf b_i(t)e^{+j2\pi\nu t}\,dt.
$$

The dimensionless $\mathbf B_i$ is the spectral row of this observation
functional. Its plus sign follows by inserting inverse Fourier synthesis
$e^{+j2\pi\nu t}$ for $\mathbf z_n(t)$; it is not the forward transform of
$\mathbf b_i$. For example, sampling channel $k$ at $t_i$ gives
$\mathbf B_i(\nu)=e^{+j2\pi\nu t_i}\mathbf e_k^T$, where $\mathbf e_k$ is
the corresponding unit coordinate vector. Insert the spectral representation
of $E[\mathbf z_n(t)\mathbf z_n(u)^H]$, with phase
$e^{j2\pi\nu(t-u)}$, into $E[n_i n_j^*]$. Interchanging the convergent
integrals gives one factor $\mathbf B_i$ and one $\mathbf B_j^H$:

$$
 C_{ij}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
 \mathbf B_i(\nu)\mathbf S_z(\nu)\mathbf B_j(\nu)^H\,d\nu.
$$

The rows include finite windows, filtering and sample-time phases; the integral
must converge. Its units are V². A white density is not a per-record variance,
and shared paths or overlapping observations need not give independent records.
Nonstationary disturbances require the covariance-kernel form of Chapter 3.
These operations construct second moments, not the Gaussian law assumed above.

Apply the **same observation** to the wanted voltage waveform. If before
observation it is $\mathbf z_s(t)=A\mathbf p(t)$ with dimensionless
$\mathbf p(t)$, then $a_i=\int\mathbf b_i(t)\mathbf p(t)\,dt$.
Filtering only the noise model while keeping the original wanted template
generally describes a different detector.

For a concrete asymmetric example, let a proper stationary scalar voltage source
$u(t)$ have density $S_0=1$ nV²/Hz on offsets $100\leq\nu\leq400$ Hz and zero
elsewhere. Let $z_1(t)=u(t)$ and $z_2(t)=g u(t-d)$, where
$g=0.7+j0.4$ and $d=0.7$ ms. Average channel 1 from 0.2 to 1.0 ms and channel 2
from 2.0 to 3.3 ms. Write their starts $t_i$ and durations $T_i$; with
$\operatorname{sinc}x=\sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)$, the combined source-to-observation
factors are

$$
 D_1(\nu)=e^{j2\pi\nu(t_1+T_1/2)}\operatorname{sinc}(\nu T_1),\qquad
 D_2(\nu)=g e^{j2\pi\nu(t_2+T_2/2-d)}\operatorname{sinc}(\nu T_2).
$$

Thus $C_{12}=S_0\int_{100}^{400}D_1(\nu)D_2(\nu)^*d\nu$
is approximately $(-113.0602-j84.8885)$ nV². The positive-offset spectrum and
unequal windows expose its complex phase; changing the sample-time sign changes
the answer. For a wanted $u_s(t)=A e^{j2\pi(250\,\mathrm{Hz})t}$ traversing these same paths,
$\mathbf a=(D_1(250),D_2(250))^T$, approximately
$(0.54987+j0.75683,-0.60897-j0.28714)^T$, rather than $(1,g)^T$.
Changing a window changes both covariance and wanted response. Recompute both
before interpreting a lower output variance as a better detection result.

The Gaussian density is proportional to
$\exp[-(\mathbf x-A\mathbf a)^H\mathbf C^{-1}(\mathbf x-A\mathbf a)]$.
The normalizing determinant is the same under the two hypotheses. Subtracting
the two quadratic exponents gives the log likelihood ratio

$$
 \log\Lambda=2A\operatorname{Re}t-A^2q,
 \qquad t=\mathbf a^H\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf x,
 \qquad q=\mathbf a^H\mathbf C^{-1}\mathbf a>0.
$$

Here $t$ has units V⁻¹ and $q$ V⁻². For these known-phase hypotheses the data enter
the likelihood ratio only through $\operatorname{Re}t$: it is a sufficient statistic
for this decision. That assertion is scoped to the declared hypotheses, not to
all possible information in $\mathbf x$. A likelihood-ratio threshold selects the
most powerful simple-hypothesis test at a specified false-alarm probability:
moving probability mass to observations with a larger density ratio can only
increase detection probability at fixed null probability.

For $\mathbf C=\sigma^2\mathbf I$, $t=\sum_m a_m^*x_m/\sigma^2$ is correlation
with the template. For time samples, the causal finite matched-filter kernel is
$h[m]=a^*[M-1-m]$ for $0\leq m<M$, zero otherwise, evaluated at sample
$M-1$, up to a known gain. Reversal aligns
the samples at that decision epoch; conjugation aligns their complex phases.
MIT's [matched-filter lecture](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-011-signals-systems-and-inference-spring-2018/dfe2855f36e44436678bfd3736c937fe_MIT6_011S18lec24.pdf),
pp. 2–5, develops the white-Gaussian detector and Gaussian-tail interpretation.
The finite complex-vector normalization above is derived here.

Normalize to $r=t/\sqrt q$, which has dimensionless proper complex Gaussian
noise variance one. Define $\rho=A^2q$. Then

$$
 Z=\sqrt2\operatorname{Re}r
 \sim\begin{cases}\mathcal N(0,1),&H_0,\\
                 \mathcal N(\sqrt{2\rho},1),&H_1.
 \end{cases}
$$

Let $\Phi$ be the standard normal CDF. A **single specified test** with
$P_{\rm FA}=\alpha$ uses $Z>\gamma$, where $\gamma=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$, and
$P_D=\Phi(\sqrt{2\rho}-\gamma)$. The factor $\sqrt2$ matters: complex variance
one gives variance one-half in each quadrature. Searching many delay, frequency
or direction cells changes the family false-alarm probability. For $K$ tests,
the union bound is $P_{\rm any}\leq K\alpha$; the exact independent-test expression
$1-(1-\alpha)^K$ requires independence, which overlapping templates rarely provide.

Detection and estimation are different outcomes. If an arbitrary complex
amplitude is to be estimated under the signal-present model, maximizing its
likelihood gives $\widehat A=t/q$ with complex error variance $1/q$. For an
unconstrained **real** amplitude it gives $\operatorname{Re}t/q$ with variance
$1/(2q)$. Enforcing nonnegative amplitude clips that estimate at zero and changes
its bias. None of those amplitude-error statements proves a desired $P_D$ or an
unambiguous phase/delay estimate.

## Colored weighting and finite accumulation {#sec-colored-extraction}

q_2(t)=0.10\cos(2\pi\,10^7t+52^\circ)\ {\rm V}.$$

To make the observation explicit, take simultaneous records from t=0 to
$T=1\ \mu$s, exactly ten IF cycles, with coefficients and phases fixed.
For these ideal tones define the extracted result as

$$z_i=\frac{2}{T}\int_0^T q_i(t)e^{-j2\pi f_It}\,dt.$$

Expanding the cosine into its two exponentials leaves a constant desired term
and a term rotating at $-2f_I$. The latter integrates to zero over ten cycles,
so this extraction gives exactly the peak-scaled envelope derived above.
The factor $2/T$ has units s$^{-1}$, leaving z in volts. A noninteger record,
frequency mismatch or varying phase need not give this result; the extraction
window then becomes part of the observation model.

Using $e^{j\alpha}=\cos\alpha+j\sin\alpha$, we obtain

$$z_1\simeq0.097815+j0.020791\ {\rm V},\qquad
z_2\simeq0.061566+j0.078801\ {\rm V}.$$

The product is

$$z_2z_1^*=0.010e^{j40^\circ}\ {\rm V}^2
 \simeq(0.007660+j0.006428)\ {\rm V}^2.$$

Its angle is 40 degrees. Across an illustrative 50-ohm resistive load, each IF
has average power $0.10^2/(2\times50)=10^{-4}$ W, or 0.10 mW.
Using $|z|^2/R$ here would incorrectly double the physical power.

The input difference is 45 degrees, while the LO difference is 12 degrees and
the added IF difference is 7 degrees. The instrument therefore reports
$45-12+7=40$ degrees. If the latter two differences are independently known,
referring the observation to P gives $40+12-7=45$ degrees modulo 360 degrees.
Without that knowledge, reporting 40 degrees as the input difference hides
an unknown receiver/reference contribution. For example, increasing both
$\Delta\phi$ and $\Delta\lambda$ by 5 degrees leaves the lower-side observation
unchanged. The output alone cannot distinguish those alternatives.

As a diagnostic counterexample, replace the LO by 1010 MHz, keep the illustrative
endpoint phases and positive-IF responses unchanged, and extract the same
positive 10 MHz IF. This is a mathematical comparison, not a promise that real
hardware retains its gain or phase after retuning. The output phases become
$-20+5-3=-18$ degrees and $-65+17+4=-44$ degrees. The reported difference is
now **−26 degrees**. Recovering the input difference requires
$\Delta\phi=\Delta\lambda+\Delta\beta-\theta=12+7-(-26)=45$ degrees.
Applying the lower-side rule would instead give $-26+12-7=-21$ degrees.
Nor is the new report simply −40 degrees: the IF path difference still adds
7 degrees. This counterexample separates spectral orientation from path phase.

## Change the reference before interpreting a change {#sec-comparison-reference}

Suppose we leave the lower-side instrument fixed and describe both extracted
channels relative to a new common IF reference with phase $\chi$.
Then $z_i'=z_i e^{-j\chi}$ and $z_2'z_1'^*=z_2z_1^*$: the comparison is
invariant. If the references instead differ by $\chi_2-\chi_1$, the reported
angle shifts by its negative. Changing output channel order similarly
conjugates the product and changes 40 degrees to −40 degrees.

A change of epoch has a related condition. For physical tones
$q_i=B_i\cos(2\pi f_i t+\gamma_i)$, setting $t=t'+t_0$ changes their phase
intercepts to $\gamma_i+2\pi f_i t_0$. The intercept difference changes by
$2\pi(f_2-f_1)t_0$. It is invariant for equal frequencies, but a frequency
mismatch makes the phase comparison evolve with time. Comparing records without
their epochs can then confuse drift with a reference change.

Moving a physical input reference plane is different from relabeling the common
IF reference. Insert 25 ps additional delay between P2 and its mixer in our
lower-side example, leaving everything else unchanged. That receiver path
contributes −9 degrees, so its output comparison changes from 40 to 31 degrees,
although the phase difference at the original P connectors is still 45 degrees.
If P2 is instead redefined downstream of that delay, its input phase is 56 degrees
and the difference at the newly named P planes is 36 degrees. The report can be
consistent in both descriptions; the quoted input result must name its planes.
At the upper-side LO, the same added RF delay changes the report from −26 to
−17 degrees. This is a useful independent sign check on the conversion model.

## What the comparison can establish {#sec-comparison-limits}

A single wrapped phase cannot establish a unique delay. Even if the entire
45-degree input difference were attributed to a pure channel-2 delay at 1 GHz,
$\Delta\phi=-360f_R\tau$ degrees gives
$\tau=-125$ ps modulo 1 ns. A positive 875 ps delay gives the same angle.
Unknown input phase and receiver offsets add further ambiguity. Delay inference
requires additional assumptions or observations across frequency; a quiet tone
comparison does not supply them.

Tracking also needs care with angle wrapping. A channel phase that goes from
179 to −179 degrees may have advanced by 2 degrees, rather than retreated by
358 degrees. Choosing that continuation requires an assumption that the true
change between valid samples has magnitude below 180 degrees, adequate signal
quality and no missing transition. Faster motion can produce the same wrapped
samples. At zero amplitude, the phase of a channel—and hence of the product—is
undefined. Near a fade, noise can dominate it. Do not join records across such
gaps or resets merely because an unwrapping routine produces a smooth curve.

For a varying signal, averaging extracted unwrapped phase and taking the angle
of an averaged complex product are different operations. The present example
avoids that distinction only because both envelopes are constant during its
specified record. A number obtained with another window, filter, epoch or
reference cannot be substituted without examining the changed observable.

The instrument can now state a precise result: in its declared settled state,
its ideal simultaneous ten-cycle extraction reports channel 2 relative to
channel 1 at O as 40 degrees with the lower LO. That calculation establishes
neither input accuracy nor temporal stability. Accuracy needs evidence about
input/reference/path errors; stability needs repeated, defined observations;
restart repeatability needs separately classified restart observations. A shared
frequency reference alone does not constrain the differential phase intercept.
Neither actual settling nor any of those performance properties has been
measured in this example.

Before proceeding, change the model yourself. Conjugate both extracted outputs
of the lower-side instrument, then predict the report and the input-referred
result. Next remove the LO and IF differential phases and repeat the comparison
with the upper LO. Finally decide whether a second 40-degree report after a
restart proves that the input phase is unchanged.

Conjugating both outputs produces −40 degrees; conjugating them back before
using the lower-side input relation recovers 45 degrees. With zero differential
LO and IF phase, the upper-side report is −45 degrees. Identical restart reports
can conceal compensating changes in input and receiver/reference phase. Each
answer follows from tracing the physical contribution, which is the reasoning
needed before stochastic stability and calibration can be developed.

The alternative continuations in @fig-phase-wrapping have identical wrapped endpoint observations. The waveform panel independently checks the delay sign. @fig-phase-validity shows why an invalid interval cannot be bridged merely by choosing the smoothest continuation.

![Synthetic wrapped-endpoint ambiguity and a delayed sinusoid. A unique continuation requires a justified intersample-motion bound.](figures/phase-wrapping.svg){#fig-phase-wrapping fig-alt="Phase can advance two degrees or retreat 358 degrees between the same observations; positive waveform delay moves a sinusoid right."}

![Schematic validity gap. Separate valid segments have no implied shared cycle count.](figures/phase-validity.svg){#fig-phase-validity fig-alt="Phase traces stop on either side of an amplitude-invalid interval, with no interpolating connection."}

## From a comparison to a receiver requirement {#sec-requirement-framing}

Before specifying “coherent channels,” state the operation the comparison must
support. A burst receiver may need a usable payload decision before its deadline;
a phase instrument may need a corrected port ratio over a stated record. Those
are different outcomes even when both contain an internal phase comparison.
A requirement should identify the observable and its units, physical/reference
planes, filtering and interval, signal/blocker envelope, operating state and
calibration history, a limit, and the evidence that could test it. An unspecified
limit remains a question, not permission to choose a convenient value.

    def test_peak_voltage_against_phase_swept_real_waveforms(self):
        for attenuation,loss in [(0,0),(30,2),(40,2),(60,2)]:
            lo,hi=model.gain_bounds(attenuation,loss)
            ps=1e-3*10**((-100-loss)/10);pb=1e-3*10**((-20-attenuation)/10)
            a=math.sqrt(100*ps);b=math.sqrt(100*pb)
            # Commensurate tones reach their worst joint peak at t=0.
            peak=max(abs(a*math.cos(2*math.pi*.7*t/10000)+b*math.cos(2*math.pi*1.3*t/10000)) for t in range(10001))
            self.assertAlmostEqual(peak*10**(hi/20),.1,places=13)
            self.assertAlmostEqual(a*10**(lo/20),math.sqrt(100e-9),places=13)
        self.assertGreater(*model.gain_bounds(0,0))
        self.assertLess(*model.gain_bounds(40,2))

    def test_spatial_aliases_and_local_finite_difference(self):
        k=2*math.pi/.3
        self.assertAlmostEqual(abs(cmath.exp(1j*k*1.2*.25)-cmath.exp(1j*k*1.2*.5)),0,places=13)
        self.assertGreater(abs(cmath.exp(1j*k*.15*.25)-cmath.exp(1j*k*.15*.5)),.7)
        th=math.pi/3;eps=1e-6
        derivative=(k*1.2*math.sin(th+eps)-k*1.2*math.sin(th-eps))/(2*eps)
        sigma=math.degrees(1/derivative/math.sqrt(100))
        self.assertAlmostEqual(sigma,.45594532639052,places=8)
        low,high=model.aperture_limits();self.assertGreater(low,high)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(cmath.exp(1j*k*high*math.sin(th)),cmath.exp(-1j*k*high*math.sin(th)),places=12)

    def test_finite_tone_observation_against_midpoint_integration(self):
        n=20000;T=.001;df=100
        average=sum(cmath.exp(2j*math.pi*df*(i+.5)*T/n) for i in range(n))/n
        self.assertAlmostEqual(abs(average)**2*100,model.requirement_case()['rho'],places=7)
        needed=model.requirement_case()['short_rho'];self.assertGreater(needed/1e5,.0025)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(needed,5321.885200828357,places=8)

    def test_branch_error_covariance_from_three_physical_noise_sources(self):
        rng=random.Random(1113);k=2*math.pi/.3;rho=model.requirement_case()['rho']
        a,b=1/(k*.15),1/(k*1.2);sd=1/math.sqrt(2*rho);n=100000
        moments=0.
        for _ in range(n):
            e0,es,el=[rng.gauss(0,sd) for _ in range(3)]
            error=a*(es-e0)-b*(el-e0);moments+=error**2
        theoretical=(a*a+b*b-a*b)/rho
        self.assertLess(abs(moments/n/theoretical-1),.018)
        self.assertLess(model.requirement_case()['branch_sum'],1e-3)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(3*14*100e6*1.1,4.62e9,places=4)
        self.assertGreater(3*14*100e6*1.25,5e9)

    def test_phase_uncertainty_against_complex_voltage_noise(self):
        rng=random.Random(321);rho=model.requirement_case()['rho'];sd=1/math.sqrt(2*rho)
        n=60000;variance=0.
        for _ in range(n):
            x=1+complex(rng.gauss(0,sd),rng.gauss(0,sd))
            y=1+complex(rng.gauss(0,sd),rng.gauss(0,sd))
            variance+=cmath.phase(y*x.conjugate())**2

# Inference, precision and ambiguity {#sec-phase-delay-inference}

A phase-sensitive receiver reports a nearly straight phase slope across frequency.
How precisely can we estimate delay, and does the fitted slope identify the delay
we actually want? These are different questions. A narrow statistical interval
can surround the wrong ambiguity branch or include an unknown receiver path.
We will derive a usable local estimator before testing its global interpretation.

The prerequisite chain is deliberate. [The phase comparison](phase-comparison.qmd)
fixes orientation and planes, [scalar stochastic phase](scalar-stochastic-phase.qmd)
separates records from ensembles and explains noise-to-phase assumptions,
[observation weighting](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd) defines the observation,
and [covariance](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) explains coupled errors and rank.
Keep their explicit local conventions: channel 2 relative to channel 1, positive
physical delay giving negative phase slope, and phase measured in radians. These
choices remain local. The calculation below is synthetic, not a measured receiver.

## Specify the observations and unknowns

At fixed input/output reference planes, measure a complex channel comparison at
$N$ known swept physical RF frequencies $f_i$ during one settled acquisition state.
The $y_i$ below are comparisons translated to the physical input-phase orientation,
not arbitrary raw positive-IF angles. For the lower-side model in Chapter 1,
$y=\theta+\Delta\lambda-\Delta\beta$; for its upper-side model,
$y=-\theta+\Delta\lambda+\Delta\beta$. Known path terms are removed in that translation;
unknown receiver delay remains a nuisance contribution to the fitted total.
This step must follow the actual conversion topology before interpreting a slope. Assume the underlying
transfer has constant amplitude above a declared validity threshold and phase
linear in frequency over this band. Let $f_0$ be the arithmetic mean of the frequencies
and $x_i=f_i-f_0$, in Hz. On a justified unwrapped branch the observations are

$$
 y_i=a+b x_i+\epsilon_i,\qquad b=-2\pi\tau.
$$

Here $a$ is phase at $f_0$, $b$ has units rad/Hz, and $\tau$ is the total differential
physical delay between the declared planes. The phase at $f_0$ is an unknown nuisance
parameter: it is needed to describe the data even when delay is the desired result.
Let errors be independent centered Gaussian with known variance $\sigma^2$ in rad²,
constant across these finite observations. Gaussian phase errors are a model,
justified only within the amplitude/SNR and unwrapping conditions discussed earlier.
A finite observation window, drift between frequency steps or correlated reference
errors can invalidate independence or the static response assumption.

An estimator is a rule taking data to a parameter estimate. Its bias is $E[\widehat\tau]-\tau$;
its variance measures scatter about its own mean; mean-square error equals variance
plus squared bias. These expectations refer to repetitions under the declared
model, not the scatter of one fitted residual sequence.

## Derive the fit from a likelihood

The likelihood treats the observed $y$ as fixed and asks how its probability density
varies with the proposed $a$ and $b$. For our Gaussian model its log, apart from a
parameter-independent constant, is

$$
 \ell(a,b)=-{1\over2\sigma^2}\sum_i(y_i-a-bx_i)^2.
$$

Maximizing this expression is equivalent to minimizing the residual sum of squares.
Differentiate with respect to $a$ and $b$ and set both derivatives to zero. Because
$\sum_i x_i=0$, the two equations separate:

$$
 \widehat a=\bar y,\qquad
 \widehat b={\sum_i x_i y_i\over S_{xx}},\qquad
 S_{xx}=\sum_i x_i^2,\qquad
 \widehat\tau=-{\widehat b\over2\pi}.
$$

At least two distinct frequencies are necessary: $S_{xx}=0$ leaves slope unidentified.
These closed forms minimize the quadratic exactly. A zero derivative need not
identify a global maximum for an arbitrary nonlinear likelihood; here the positive
quadratic curvature supplies that conclusion. For known unequal variances, the
Gaussian log likelihood instead weights each squared residual by its inverse
variance. The mean frequency must then be weighted too. This precision weighting
and the hazards of estimated weights are discussed in the
[NIST regression handbook](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/pmd/section1/pmd143.htm).
For correlated data the quadratic is $r^TC^{-1}r$, with positive-definite known $C$;
whitening means applying a fixed transform $W$ with $WCW^T=I$ so transformed
errors have unit covariance. Its stable construction and coupled fitting are
extensions beyond this bounded scalar derivation. We do not assume that
relabeling samples makes their covariance diagonal.

Substituting the signal model into the fit shows its noise contribution directly:

$$
 \widehat b-b={\sum_i x_i\epsilon_i\over S_{xx}},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}\widehat\tau={\sigma^2\over4\pi^2 S_{xx}},\qquad
 \operatorname{var}\widehat a={\sigma^2\over N}.
$$

Both estimates are unbiased in this unwrapped linear model and their covariance
is zero because $\sum_i x_i=0$. Changing the intercept reference to another frequency
changes its covariance with slope; it does not change the physical delay estimate.
The equations reveal the design lever: spread in observation frequency, not merely
sample count, controls local delay precision.

## What an information bound actually bounds

## Derive sensitivity and retain covariance

Let $p$ be a vector of input quantities, $p_0$ its nominal value and $\delta p$ a centered
small perturbation with covariance $C_p$. For the following quadratic-order
remainder, assume $h$ is twice continuously differentiable with bounded second
derivatives throughout the relevant scaled input region. Taylor expansion gives

$$
 h(p_0+\delta p)=h(p_0)+g\,\delta p+O(\|\delta p\|^2),\qquad
 g_i={\partial h\over\partial p_i}\bigg|_{p_0}.
$$

The row $g$ contains sensitivity coefficients. After declaring compatible coordinate
scales, its entries carry output units per input unit. Expanding the variance
of the first-order term yields

$$
 \operatorname{var}h\simeq g C_p g^T
 =\sum_i g_i^2 C_{ii}+2\sum_{i<j}g_i g_j C_{ij}.
$$

This is Chapter 4's quadratic form applied to the linearized output. It is exact
for an affine $h$, otherwise approximate. The first neglected mean correction is
one half the sum of Hessian entries $H_{ij}=\partial^2h/(\partial p_i\partial p_j)$
times $C_{ij}$, provided the second-order expansion has an integrable remainder
small relative to retained terms over the input distribution. For example, bounded
third derivatives throughout its support and a sufficiently small third absolute
perturbation moment control that remainder. Differentiability alone does not
justify a quadratic remainder: $h(x)=|x|^{3/2}$ at zero has zero derivative but a
remainder larger than order $x^2$.
This warns that $h(E[p])$ need not equal $E[h(p)]$. Covariance-aware first-order
uncertainty propagation and inclusion of significant measurement-process inputs
are also specified in [NIST TN 1297, Appendix A.1–A.3](https://www.nist.gov/pml/nist-technical-note-1297/nist-tn-1297-appendix-law-propagation-uncertainty).
The theorem does not supply a missing physical input model.

A covariance may describe repeated receiver variability, uncertainty about a
fixed path parameter, or uncertainty of an estimator. These are different
ensembles or states of knowledge. Identify which is intended before combining
them. A confidence or coverage claim also requires distributional assumptions;
standard deviation alone does not specify a tail probability. A full measurement
uncertainty procedure and calibration evidence belong to later metrology work.

## Follow the delay budget through a changed assumption
# Physical noise, blockers and timing disturbances {#sec-physical-disturbances}

A quiet terminated-input receiver can become noisy when an antenna, another
channel or a strong blocker is connected. Which physical source changed, and
through which path did its disturbance enter the reported observation? An
arbitrary covariance matrix cannot answer that question. Nor can a clock-jitter
number evaluated only at the wanted carrier.

This treatment constructs sources before combining them. The reader should be
able to convert thermal source voltage into delivered power, construct a coupled
noise matrix from a circuit or incident field, derive a blocker-dependent LO or
filter constraint, and test timing error against the complete analog waveform.
[Chapters 2–4](covariance-quadratic-forms.qmd) supply stochastic and matrix tools;
[Chapter 8](fields-geometry-transduction.qmd) supplies loaded field-to-port maps.
We use its fixed-configuration, orientation-normalized linear receiver interface.
All component values, spectra and targets below are synthetic teaching inputs.
None is a device guarantee or measured receiver result.

## Sources, loading and delivered noise {#sec-loaded-noise}

Keep two representations distinct. For a real centered stationary voltage $e(t)$,
use two-sided $S_e(f)$ over signed physical frequency $f$, in V²/Hz, with
$E[e^2]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}S_e(f)\,df$. A resistor $R$ at temperature $T$
has the classical open-circuit thermal model

$$
 S_e(f)=2k_BT R,
$$

over a finite band where resistance is approximately real, equilibrium holds and
$h_P|f|\ll k_BT$. Here $k_B=1.380649\times10^{-23}$ J/K is Boltzmann's constant
and $h_P$ denotes Planck's constant. The classical model is not extended to
infinite bandwidth. Analog Devices [MT-047](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-047.pdf),
Rev. 0, p. 2 gives RMS voltage $\sqrt{4k_BTRB}$ for a one-sided bandwidth $B$;
the two-sided density above divides its positive-frequency density by two.

Attach a noiseless real load $R_L$. Circuit division gives
$S_{v_L}=2k_BTR\,[R_L/(R+R_L)]^2$ and $S_{p_L}=S_{v_L}/R_L$ W/Hz at signed
physical frequency. A real RF passband of positive-frequency width $B$ has a
negative-frequency image of equal width. For $R_L=R$, integrating both bands
gives delivered noise power $k_BTB$. At 290 K and $B=100$ kHz this is
$4.00388\times10^{-16}$ W, or approximately $-123.98$ dBm. Replacing the matched
load by $R_L=4R$ gives only $16/25=0.64$ of the matched power even though its
voltage is larger. High noise voltage and high delivered noise power are different
statements. The “noiseless load” computes only the source's contribution; a real
resistor load has its own thermal source and must be included when relevant.

For a peak-scaled complex envelope $z$ around positive carrier $f_c$, the local
analytic-signal construction instead gives $S_z(\nu)=4S_e(f_c+\nu)$ over its
retained offset band. The factor four comes from doubling positive-frequency
amplitude before shifting it to baseband. At a matched load this gives
$S_{z_L}=2k_BTR$, and power density $S_{z_L}/(2R)=k_BT$. This translation recovers
the same $k_BTB$ with one complex-envelope band of width $B$. It is a local
normalization declaration, not a new book-wide PSD default. Never add real
two-sided voltage densities to peak-envelope densities without translating them.

An active input also has internal disturbance sources. A selective equivalent
model uses an input-referred series voltage $e_n$ and current $i_n$ delivered
into an effective source impedance $Z_s$ with a declared positive direction.
Define the sensed equivalent noise as $n=e_n+Z_si_n$. At each frequency,

$$
 S_n=S_e+|Z_s|^2S_i+2\operatorname{Re}\{Z_s^*S_{ei}\},\qquad
 S_{ei}(f)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}E[e_n(t+\tau)i_n(t)^*]e^{-j2\pi f\tau}\,d\tau.
$$

This follows by expanding $|E_n+Z_sI_n|^2$; the cross-spectrum ordering is the
same $X Y^*$ convention as Chapter 3. It requires $|S_{ei}|^2\leq S_eS_i$.
The equivalent source locations and the impedance seen by them must be derived
from the actual input topology, including loading and reverse coupling. MT-047
pp. 1–3 supports the voltage/current-source representation and impedance
sensitivity; its simplified op-amp independence assumption is not a general RF
LNA model. Equal data-sheet noise figures do not supply a multichannel covariance.

For example, independent Poisson arrivals of charge $q$ at rate $\lambda=I/q$
produce, after removing the mean current, two-sided shot-noise density
$q^2\lambda=qI$ A²/Hz in the ideal impulse/current model. A finite pulse response
multiplies this by its squared normalized transform. MT-047 p. 2 gives the
corresponding one-sided $2qI$ form for suitable input junctions and cautions
against inferring it from net bias current in compensated circuits. Correlated
transport, excess noise and device bandwidth change that model. A flicker term
$K/|f|$ likewise needs lower and upper cutoffs and an evidence-based coefficient;
integrating it to zero frequency does not define a finite stationary variance.
Those are source-model boundaries, not problems that an optimizer can cure.

## Coupled networks and external fields {#sec-physical-covariance}

Stack physical source amplitudes into $\mathbf u$, give their cross-spectral
matrix $\mathbf S_u$, and solve the loaded circuit to obtain $\mathbf n=\mathbf T\mathbf u$.
Then

$$
 \mathbf S_n=\mathbf T\mathbf S_u\mathbf T^H.
$$

Chapter 4 owns this propagation identity. The engineering work here is deciding
what $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf T$ physically contain. A common source uses one
column reaching multiple outputs. Mutually independent local sources have a
diagonal source matrix, but a nondiagonal transfer can still correlate outputs.
Conversely, device-internal source correlations belong in $\mathbf S_u$.
Positive semidefiniteness checks admissible second moments; it does not establish
that the chosen source powers and paths describe hardware.

Consider a reciprocal resistive two-port: each port connects through a 10-ohm
series resistor to a shared node; that node connects through another 10-ohm
resistor to ground. Both loads are noiseless 50-ohm observation loads. All three
source resistors are at 290 K. Equivalent series-noise sources have their
positive terminal facing the observation port for the two arms, and facing
the shared node for the return resistor. Open-circuit noise voltages are
$\mathbf v_{\rm oc}=(e_1+e_0,e_2+e_0)^T$, with independent resistor sources
$S_{e_0}=S_{e_1}=S_{e_2}=2k_BT(10\ \Omega)$. Its impedance and source matrices are

$$
 \mathbf Z_A=\begin{pmatrix}20&10\\10&20\end{pmatrix}\ \Omega,
 \qquad \mathbf S_{\rm oc}=2k_BT
 \begin{pmatrix}20&10\\10&20\end{pmatrix}\ \Omega.
$$

The off-diagonal term has a physical cause: the same resistor $e_0$ reaches
both ports. The open-circuit vector is defined with both loads disconnected;
the drawn loads apply only when calculating $\mathbf v_L$. This is a constructed circuit demonstration of thermal coupling,
not asserted antenna/LNA data. @fig-loaded-noise-paths shows the shared return
and the source decomposition used in the calculation.

![Three independent thermal sources become correlated open-circuit port voltages through a shared resistive return. Loading then changes both variance and covariance. The noiseless loads isolate these three source contributions.](figures/loaded-noise-paths.svg){#fig-loaded-noise-paths fig-alt="Ports 1 and 2 each connect through a 10 ohm resistor to one common node, which returns through a third 10 ohm resistor to ground. Each port has a noiseless 50 ohm load. The shared resistor source e0 enters both open-circuit voltages; local e1 and e2 enter separately."}

With $\mathbf Z_L=50\mathbf I\ \Omega$, the Chapter 8 loading equation gives

$$
 \mathbf L={50\over4800}
 \begin{pmatrix}70&-10\\-10&70\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 {\mathbf S_L\over2k_BT}=
 \begin{pmatrix}9.33160&2.38715\\2.38715&9.33160\end{pmatrix}\ \Omega.
$$

The symmetric common voltage $(v_1+v_2)/\sqrt2$ sees impedance 30 ohms and
loading gain $50/(30+50)=0.625$; the differential voltage
$(v_2-v_1)/\sqrt2$ sees 10 ohms and gain $50/(10+50)=5/6$. Their spectral
coefficients after dividing by $2k_BT$ are respectively 11.71875 and 6.94444
ohms. Transforming those independent mode powers back gives the matrix above.
This second derivation also checks loading and the sign of the covariance.

For the unnormalized difference $d=v_2-v_1$, the true density is
$S_d/(2k_BT)=13.88889\ \Omega$. Using just the two diagonal entries as if they
were independent predicts 18.66319 ohms, an overestimate of 34.375 percent.
